title: The Xi'an stele (781)
hook: a stone in China records the luminous religion brought by Syriac-speaking monks

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Thomas Christians of Kerala, and your line was thomas went east. Did you find Kerala on the map? Today the road keeps going east. Day seven hundred ninety-eight.

A tall slab of dark stone stands in a museum in Xi'an, in China. It rests on the back of a carved stone tortoise. At the top, carved small, there's a cross, rising out of clouds and a lotus flower. Below it, columns of Chinese characters run down the face, and along the bottom and edges there's a second script, Syriac, the language of the churches of the East. The Chinese title calls it a memorial to the spread of the luminous religion in China. The stone tells how a teaching came east to China, carried by monks with books. Today's word is the stone.

Here's the story the stone tells, in paraphrase. A monk named Alopen came from the West, from a land the Chinese called Daqin, carrying scriptures and images. He arrived at the capital, Chang'an, the city we now call Xi'an. The emperor Taizong sent an official to welcome him, had his scriptures translated in the palace library, questioned him about the teaching, and then issued a decree allowing it to be taught. Monasteries were built. The stone then gives a summary of the faith, and this is the part that rewards slow reading. It speaks of one true God, of the Messiah born of a virgin, of a bright star announcing the birth, and of Persians who saw it and came with gifts. That's the wise men, told in Chinese. It speaks of baptism by water and of the cross. And it does all this in words borrowed from the religious language already living in China, some of it Buddhist, some Daoist. The monks didn't invent a new vocabulary. They reached for the words people already prayed with. Even the name they chose, the luminous teaching, is a word about light. The stone also records hard times, when the community was mocked and opposed, and then times of renewed favor. It was carved later than Alopen's arrival, as a look back on what had grown. The monks belonged to the Church of the East, and this stone lets that church speak for itself, in two scripts. This week the path has gone a long way: Caedmon singing after a dream in the stable, Cuthbert by the sea, Bede finishing his work, then Ethiopia, Armenia, Kerala, and now China. The church of these centuries was not one place. It was many roads.

Here's the practice: look at a map of the Silk Road. If you have your phone, search for one now and keep it in front of you. If not, draw one in your mind: the Mediterranean on the left, China on the right, and in between, deserts, mountains, oasis towns, Persia, Central Asia. Settle, and breathe. Follow the line with your eyes or your finger, slowly, from west to east, the way a monk with books and a walking stick might have gone. Notice how long it is. If you pray, you can pray for the Christians who live along that road today, and for everyone else who lives there too. The bell holds the time.
The Xi'an stele. A carved stone in China that tells how monks of the Church of the East brought the luminous teaching to the emperor's capital.
Your line: the luminous teaching. Today, notice one word you use for something holy, and ask where you borrowed it from. Day seven hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Christians of the Assyrian Church of the East and related churches remember the monks who carried their faith along the Silk Road, and the Xi'an stele is studied and visited as a record of that history.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old stone in a museum.
what it means: a record, in Chinese and Syriac, of monks bringing Christianity to the Tang capital and an emperor allowing it.
what a scholar hears: the Church of the East, written in borrowed Buddhist and Daoist words: the luminous teaching on the Silk Road.

notes: The title carries the date 781 from the index; the spoken script states no date. The index hook gives 635 for Alopen's arrival; it is left out of the spoken script per the claims rule. Confirm both.

Physical description (tortoise base, cross rising from clouds and a lotus, Syriac along the bottom and sides, now in the Beilin/Stele Forest Museum in Xi'an): not from the inscription's text; confirm or trim.

Inscription summary (Alopen from Daqin, welcomed by Taizong's minister, scriptures translated in the palace library, imperial edict, monasteries; one God, virgin birth, star, Persians with gifts, baptism, cross; later opposition and renewed favor) paraphrased from the stele; Legge's 1888 translation is public domain and could be quoted after checking.
'Borrowed words... some Buddhist, some Daoist' reflects common scholarly reading of the text; confirm.
The name 'Nestorian' is disputed by the Assyrian Church of the East; the script says 'Church of the East'. Confirm.
'Reached across Persia and Central Asia along the trade roads' is a general historical statement; confirm.
